CB SPECIAL: The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela

By: Nikola Vrahimis | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche Nelson Mandela

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon.

Unique Selling Point:
For 27 years of Mandela’s life in prison his sole source of comfort, his only contact with his family and friends was the occasional visit and letters…letters he received and letters he wrote.
From the very beginning Mandela was a prolific letter writer with both personal and official letters. Every letter was copied into an A4 hard covered notebook. These have been stored in boxes locked away in the State Archives. In celebration of Mandela’s 100th Birthday they are finally seeing the light of day.


Summary:
On July 18th, Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela would have turned 100 years. This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon.

For the best part of 10 years the Nelson Mandela Foundation and South African National Archives have been collecting and assembling letters written by Nelson Mandela during his 27 years incarceration. Poignant, impassioned, gripping and always inspirational the letters – many of them never seen before by the public - provide new insight into how Mandela maintained his inner spirits while living in almost complete isolation and how he engaged with the outside world that became increasingly outraged by his plight as his imprisonment dragged into its fourth decade.

A landmark book, *“The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” - the first and only authorised and authenticated collection of correspondence spanning the 27 years Mandela was held as a political prisoner - will be released a week before Mandela’s Birthday. In perfect synchronicity our documentary Mandela 100 will reveal some of the most poignant, the most witty, the most dramatic of his letters.



Further information:
The documentary will follow three main threads throughout its 48 minutes. Interviews with some of the younger members of the Mandela family and other individuals who featured in his life will be seamlessly weaved together to a new reveal of Nelson Mandela, the man and the life he lived.

Firstly, we will trace Mandela’s life through the bigger landscape of world events, telescoping in to events where they might have influenced Mandela or the political stage he played on …for example the lead up to and the release of Mandela came at a time of extreme global change, most notably Gorbachev was dismantling the Soviet Union; in 1989 the Berlin wall fell…..Destruction of the old, heralded new beginnings.

Secondly we will trace Mandela through the different stages of his life.
‘Mandela 100’ will showcase the seven stages of Nelson Mandela
1 Rolihlahla – or Trouble maker as it means: Portraying his earliest and most deeply rooted influences. The imprint of language, place and culture lie in his traditional upbringing in rural Transkei.
2 Nelson: His early years as a schoolboy and the ‘colonial’ name he was given. Embracing a colonial education, Nelson Mandela’s enduring respect for Anglo-Saxon culture is rooted in his early encounters with mission schooling, the British notions of ‘fair play’ and doing things ‘properly’ remain with him throughout his life.
3 Mr Mandela: Mandela makes his way to Johannesburg where he initially feels very much an outsider but he will soon become a charming ‘man about town’, a confident legal professional and a committed political activist.
4: Comrade, Military Commander, Fugitive: Mandela becomes a firebrand ANC leader and military commander. He goes underground, is arrested and becomes accused No 1 in the Rivonia Trial. His political activism comes at a huge personal cost.
5 Prisoner 46664: Prison shapes Mandela, inside and out. Given the harshness of prison life and the length of his incarceration, it is intriguing that he later looks back on his years in prison with some nostalgia. In a sense he remains a prisoner throughout his life, a prisoner of fame and towards the end of his life a prisoner of infirmity.
6 Mr President: With Chris Hani’s murder in April 1993 and South Africa teetering on the brink of chaos, Mandela effectively steps in to lead the country. After the first democratic elections his time as leader sparks a renewal in South Africa with the rainbow nation celebrated with optimism both locally and abroad.
7 Madiba: Post 1999, the Madiba legacy, the good, the bad and the ugly. We explore the enduring legacy of Madiba but also bring new questions to the fore as a new generation is not so enamoured with the Madiba legacy, branding him a sellout.

Thirdly – the new reveal of the multitude of letters he would pen to loved ones, compatriots, prison authorities and government officials. At first he was only allowed to write and receive one letter of 500 words every six months. Even when restrictions were finally loosened regarding the length and regularity of his correspondence, his jailors continued censoring his letter for political overtones – even innocuous references.

The letters will provide an intimate portrait of a political activist who was at once a devoted husband, adoring father, dedicated student (studying for a law degree behind bars) and abiding friend.

A father of five when he was sentenced to life imprisonment, his letters became a critical means of parenting in absentia – particularly as he was denied visiting rights until his children reached the age of 16. Letters to comrades and old acquaintances are infused with optimism and warmth, as well as a steely resolve to stay the course. Mandela reminisces and often frets over the future yet never loses hope.

‘Mandela 100’ the documentary will get the back story of some of the most intimate, most revealing, most dramatic of these letters. Co- Author, Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela, Madiba’s granddaughter will be one of the interviews to navigate us through the letters. Some of the other interviews we aim to get from recipients of his letters or their family as the case may be…Ndaba Mandela, grandson of Mandela; the nurse who took care of Madiba in hospital; Nqaba Ngoyi ( great grandson of the late Lilian Ngoyi who he wrote to.); Tim Wilson, son-in law of the late Bram Fischer; Zwai Kente, Mandela’s nephew and son of the renowned playwright Gibson; fellow prisoner, Mac Maharaj (Mandela wrote to his wife, Tim Maharaj) the De Waals, friends of Winnie Mandela from her Brandfort days; the Tambo family (Adelaide Tambo was a recipient of letters; Tony Eprile ( son of Cecile Eprile, Golden Post editor); Andile Xaba ( son of the late Nike, Winnies sister and Marshall Xaba.

Mandela in his letters is witty, clever (often cloaking references to banned colleagues through nicknames) and empathetic with others despite his own tribulations and tragedies, like the death of his mother and son, over which he anguished.

And a new portrait emerges of his close relationship with Winnie Madikizela-Mandela whose own battle with the apartheid system during the same period is documented dramatically through their letters.

Press Release:

Journalist Sam Venter and Mandela’s granddaughter Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela have collaborated on “ The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” released in honour of his 100th.



Script:


Mandela Letters Script 48 min

Title: 23 June 1969 Nelson Mandela to his Daughter’s Zenani and Zindzi
Swati:
Once again our beloved Mummy has been arrested and now she and Daddy are away in jail my heart bleeds as I think of her sitting in some police cell far away from home for long you may like orphans without your own home or parents, now you will get no birthday or Christmas presents ….gone are comfortable beds the warm blankets and clean linen she used to provide in house no 8115 in Orlando West the one place in the world that is so dear to our hearts

V/O 14 sec
For 27 years of Nelson Mandela’s life in prison his sole source of comfort, his only contact with his family and friends was the occasional visit and letters…letters he received and letters he wrote.

The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela

Swati:
My first memories are what my mom told me that he loved us very much and that he was in prison fighting for the country. She said it was a sacrifice that he chose to make
It was always sad for my mom she essentially was an orphan both of them were orphans so I can imagine what that’s like as a child experiencing the abandonment and not having parents around and trying to reconcile the fact they are doing this for a cause but when you are a child you don’t care you just want your parents around.

V/O 9 sec
When Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela was born, her grandfather had already spent 17 years on Robben Island.

Title: 23 June 1969 Nelson Mandela to his Daughter’s Zenani and Zindzi
Check pic Winnie and Nelson in Graphic
Do not worry my darling s we have a lot of friends they will look after you and one day Mummy and Daddy will return and you will no longer be orphans without a home and then we will all live peacefully and happily as all normal families do
With lots of love and many kisses
Yours affectionately
Daddy

Swati
I don’t think he could have survived it unless he had that attitude that was required of him to make it though the time. and I think that’s what kept him going.

Title: Rivonia Trial 12 June 1964
Up Sound; I have fought……..harmony.

V/O 13 and a half sec
With Mandela’s closing address echoing through apartheid South Africa, Mandela and his fellow prisoners set foot on South Africa’s most notorious prison on a bitterly cold winter’s morning.

Title: Robben Island 13 June 1964

Mac
The regime had decided that imprisoning us on Robben was to make sure the public forgot us, and initially we were put in the lowest category of the prisoners the D group so we were only allowed one visit every 6 months and one letter I think of 500 words and they carried that out rigourously to the point where first they would obliterate using ball point words to cancel out what you had said sometimes you would get a letter which virtually said Dear so and so ended up with your loved one just signing it and nothing else so how important was letters or visits they were our soul life line.

V/O 20 sec
From the very beginning Mandela was a prolific letter writer. Every letter, be it personal or official, was copied into an A4 hard covered notebook. These have been stored in boxes locked away in the State Archives. They are finally being revealed to the public.

V/O 12 sec
Journalist Sam Venter and Mandela’s granddaughter Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela have collaborated on “The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” released in honour of his 100th birthday.

Sahm :
Madiba essentially wrote this book 98% of it is in his own words unmediated written at the time so we have him speaking to us still 5 years after his passing.
Swati PIC MANDELA
He was isolated and many people forgot about who he was and what he was doing and why he was doing, so I think it will give people a deeper insight into why we have the freedom we have and how we got the freedom we got.

V/O 8 sec
Mandela’s letters were his only way of raising his children, trying to maintain a relationship with them.

Title: To Makaziwe Mandela, his eldest daughter 1 May 1970

My Darling
In your undated letter which reached me on the 5th November last year you say that you no longer want to be a scientist because funds will not be available for you to study for this profession, I will do everything in my power to organise the funds required for your degree studies.

Swati
He was trying to parent his children from Robben Island and trying to provide as much support as he could with the limited resources that he could. I could feel this desperation just to be there and support them and support my grandmother and what she was going through and then his children and all of his children and then really not having the ability to do so.

To Winnie Mandela, his wife 2.4.69
To me the portrait aroused mixed feeling you look somewhat sad, absent minded and unwell but lovely all the same the devastating beauty and charm which 10 stormy years of married life have not chilled I suspect that you intended the portrait to convey a special message that no words could ever express…rest assured I have caught it.

V/O 11 sec
Even letters to Winnie were not assured of reaching her; some letters would get through, some would not, some were censored, all at the whim of the prison authorities.

Mandela Up SOUND: One of the saddest….and that was the case.

Mac
He was just called to the office and he came back he went straight to his cell all of us sensed there was something wrong here so it is Sisulu that went to his cell sat there with him and a long time later Sisulu and said Comrades Madiba’s mother has passed away please don’t crowd him, when you went into his cell you find Madiba had wrapped himself in his blanket yes you are with your comrades it is ok to cry but if you did that the regimes wardens are watching and that would be shown as a weakness.

V/O 7 sec
He was not allowed to attend her burial. Then a year later his son Thembi died in a car accident.

Sahm
You can just imagine what it must have been like, your son is killed and you can’t reach out…

Small Title: To Evelyn Mandela : his former wife and mother of Thembi 16 07 69
I write to give you, Makatho and Maki my deepest sympathy I know more than anyone living today just how devastating this cruel blow must be for Thembi was your first born and the second child you have lost….

Sahm
He didn’t even get a response to his application to attend his son’s funeral, it was just ignored so this is when you have to rely on the depth of your character and dignity so this is where you have to rely on the depths of your strength of character and your own dignity.

Mac
That episode and those reactions of Mandela are a mirror of what was happening to everyone else…. My father died while I was in prison I only learnt of his death months later We came to realise … we had community of prisoners when you faltered you had your comrades to help you, to pick you up there was your family they could not tell you what was happening to them…

V/O 7 sec
Denis Goldberg, the only white man convicted in the Rivonia Trial, was sent to Pretoria Prison.

Denis 1/5554
They built a special prison for us actually with hot and cold running water and flush toilet instead of a stinking pot but prison’s prison you know.

V/O 5 sec
Sentenced to life, Denis decided his wife, at least, should be free.

Denis
I wrote to her to say I want you to live your life to the fullest extent you wish. I might never se you again and I say this not because I reject you again but because I love you, I’m in prison it does not mean you had to be, I can say it took 13 years to the point when I woke up absolutely free of jealousy what you say intellectually and believe to be right is not emotional. I think all of our wives and children paid the price to an extent we in prison were freed from we had no choices about eroticism about being loved and softness and gentleness not easy mot easy.

Part 1 ends 11 15. 10


PART 2 The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela

V/O
While Mandela was incarcerated his famiiy’s life became difficult and often dangerous. In May 1969 Winnie was hauled from her house in the dead of night. She spent the following fourteen months in solitary confinement… With no idea of who was looking after their children, Mandela reached out to Winnie’s sister.

To Niki Xaba, Winnies sister 15. 7. 69
The tender faces of small children distorted by fear & drowsiness seeing their dear mother escorted away in the dead of night and unable to understand the issues involved is a memory that could haunt the most fearless mother.

Andile
My mother was devoted to her family their mother died when they were young so my mother as the eldest sister assumed a kind of motherly role Winnie was one of my mother’s younger sister. In the street where we lived don’t want to attract attention from the police.

Swati.
My grandmother used to say it was unpopular to be a Mandela, it’s popular now but then it wasn’t so for them to be taken in by people was a big ask for a lot of people because a lot of people didn’t want to be associated with the family at the time.

V/O 13 sec
Despite the relentless censorship Mandela’s correspondence never abated. All the hundreds of letters he wrote, be they to family, friends or government officials, were copied into separate notebooks.

Mac
There were some comrades who had a variety of reasons for making copies. One was to keep everything alive in your mind so the correspondence of once in 6 months became a conversation with whom you were writing to.

Andile
By keeping the records, he was aware he was writing for the future He knew apartheid wouldn’t last and he would out live apartheid and that’s the greatest gift we have from him.

Mac
Madiba had a great sense of history he had a great sense that what we were doing should be bequeathed to others to carry on the struggle and there was no carbon paper we were not allowed carbon paper. In fact, we were not allowed to make copies of those letters.

V/O 9 sec
In 1966, Michael Dingake joined the other political prisoners on Robben Island. Newcomers brought news.

Michael
There was one thing about us as prisoners we were confident that one day we were going to be free the fight was on although we were not allowed newspapers we were able to read newspapers smuggled sometimes you got news after 2 months anything, the boycott the sanctions we knew about it.

V/O 7 and a half sec
And Nelson Mandela determined his role as leader, taking up other prisoner’s problems or grievances.

Michael
Nelson was a consistent fighter if he didn’t agree with something he took up and he was regarded as the leader by the outside, by the international community.

V/O 10 and a half sec
Less than 5 years into the Rivonia Trialist’s sentences, Mandela wrote to the Minister of Justice demanding their release on the basis that they were political prisoners.

To The Minister of Justice 22 4 69
Parliament Buildings
Cape Town
Dear Sir
………. At the outset we wish to point out that in making this application we are not pleading for mercy but exercising the inherent right of all people incarcerated for their political beliefs.

Mac
We were building a written record of all the efforts that we were making to find a way to engage with the government of the day and ensure it engaged with the liberation and the ANC in particular.

V/O 19 sec
In their letters Mandela and his fellow prisoners were not allowed to make any political reference. Letters to people with political connections were forbidden. Often they simply never arrived at their destination. So writing in code was part and parcel of being a political prisoner on the island.

Mac
Our spouses were also political activists and therefore they understood the code language In the Mandela letters you will find reference to Number 1 so in his letter to Winnie he would refer to her by Xhosa word first and Winnie understood it was Ruth First

V/O 8 sec
In the archives Sahm came across a letter that the censors had held back…addressed to a Gcwanini Miya.

Sahm
…. All I could work out these these were two Clan names belonging to someone, and in the process of making this book we used to go and sit with Winnie Mandela. and this one day I showed her this letter who was this person and without missing a beat she said that’s Duma Nokwe, Adv Duma Nokwe.

V/O 18 sec
Advocate Duma Nokwe was elected Secretary General of the ANC in 1958. In 1963 he went into exile in Zambia.
Nosizwe Macamo is the youngest of his children. She was only 3 years old when she and her sisters joined their parents in exile.

Nosizwe
We had to be taken out of SA by people we didn’t know, so we were passed
from one comrade to the next comrade to the next in the bush on foot on bicycles through Botswana where we eventually met my mother in who had left prior to our leaving us because the situation was so dire so that was how we left SA so nobody sort of left on a jet plane.

V/O 9 and a half sec
Duma Nokwe died in 1978. He never received any letters Mandela wrote. His family only found out about this letter just over a year ago.

Sahm
They were so happy that Madiba had written to him and one of the questions was so here is this freedom fighter writing to another freedom fighter both of them lawyers and he’s writing about singing and dancing.

Title: To Duma Nokwe ( Gcwanini Miya) 1.1..77 Full Quality ???
Our Dear Gcwanini
Now its even more difficult to follow cultural events on the mainland and even cautious comment would literally be to rush in where angels fear to tread…..
Any way three musicals seem to have attracted a lot of attention recently namely. Umababatha Ipi Tombi & Meropa all of them seem tremendous in print.

Nosizwe
You thinking here is this man sitting in jail and he is writing about theatre and this and that ……. We came to the conclusion then this was a code but try as we might we couldn’t decipher anything…

Nosizwe reads
its said to have broken all records in Johannesburg when it ran for 122 weeks…
and was seen by 500 thousand people I also understand in London it had similar success and three companies are presently performing in several continents.

Nosizwe: Such detail and some of the words you think what was that.

PART 3

The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela

V/O 20 sec
In the late 60’s conditions began to improve, after a visit from Opposition Member of Parliament Helen Suzman. Prisoners were now allowed to receive and write one letter, and receive visitors, every three months.

Amina Cachalia’s son Ghaleb was a young boy when Mandela was sent to Robben Island.

Ghaleb
I am sitting here scores of letters written in Nelson’s tiny print and he say’s

You say you and Yusuf are lonely people without the kids since when K was 5 was m was 4 when I last saw you but the baby you nursed on your lap was neither K or the sister but my friend Yusuf the giant. It’s never wise for those who are inside to fight against those who are free

V/O 5 sec
Yusuf and Amina Cachalia were friends and comrades with Mandela in the struggle.

Ghaleb
There was always political talk in the dining room the kitchen and Mandela’s name always was present I was 4/5 year’s old that’s when I began to remember things, and I can recall the excitement in the 70’s when a letter would arrive and my parents would read it and scour it for hidden meaning and the like.

Ghaleb
I also think that there were probably political reasons for that the letters went to my mum and not my dad because my dad was clearly house arrested during that period and I suppose he wanted the letters to come across as a family friendly letter but as always hidden messages put into the letters.

To Joyce Sikhhakane : comrade of Winnie Mandela. January 1 1971
My dear Nomvula
For you and John is it true can you two really do this to me without so much as giving me a hint a hint missed heaps of meat and pudding at the engagement party

V/O 15 sec
Mandela’s letter to struggle activist and journalist Joyce Sikhakane-Rankin, whom he calls Nomvula, is infectious in its sense of joy and celebration. Joyce was marrying John Faduna, a relative of his.

… To you wedding I would have been accepted just as I am, without having to sport a frock coat, starched shirt & top hat. What is even more important to me, your wedding is one occasion where I could have shined at last. I rehearse daily on a penny whistle with more practice I could have tried Handels Messiah on it on the great day.

V/ O 12 and a half sec Change graphic people to black check people visuals
But Mandela’s congratulations were premature. He was only to know later that the Special Branch called her out for breaking her banning order; they said the marriage was invalid.

Joyce
They said they were going to charge me…So the marriage was invalid…because I had broken the banning orders that’s the way they interpreted it.
You feel dammed what ever they say you are dammed, I just continued with my life,

V/O 12 sec
In his letters to prison authorities Mandela insisted prisoners’ rights were upheld …and the degradation of black prisoners was a cause he fiercely pursued.

The Commissioner of Prisons 12th July 1976
Pretoria
In this country only white prisoners have the right to sleep in pyjamas…Black prisoners here sleep naked with only blankets as a cover…For thirteen years I have slept naked on a cement floor that becomes damp and cold during the rainy season.

Andile
It was just a system that de humanising him and he refused he said I want pyjamas I want long trousers.

V/O 7 and a half sec
It was in their deliberate isolation of the political prisoners, that the South African apartheid regime made a crucial mistake.

Mac
Instead of dispersing us throughout the prison system it put us together and it had common law prisoners there to do cooking of food and all that when it found we were communicating with them and finding sympathy with them, it removed them too. when they removed them what else was left except to study intensely what was happening both to equip yourselves so that when you got released you went into battle and those who left behind to continue teaching the others and share the knowledge.

V/O 11 sec
On May the 16th 1977, Winnie Mandela was banished to the dusty town of Brandfort in the Orange Free State. She was there for 8 years.

Sahm: This book for me is full of all sorts of serendipities links and when Winnie Mandela was banished to Brandfort, Piet De Waal was the town lawyer and his wife `Adele befriended Winnie and was incredibly helpful to her in this horrible hostile situation.

Meyer: My mother invited her to the house and Winnie came to the house and my mother came to the door and said this is my house please come and make use of the music and books and make yourself comfortable.

V/O 14 and a half sec
It’s easy to forget the laws that kept South Africans living apart, like the curfew. In Brandfort a siren went off just before 9pm …and every black person that didn’t live in the backyard of a white house, had to be out of town.

Meyer
If you think back maybe you can say it was brave but I think they were just oblivious of black and white for them it was a person who came from a different environment …I don’t think she had running water, it was like dumping her into a terrible space and my mother realised that here is a person in need …

To Adele de Waal, a friend of his wife Winnie Mandela 29.8.83

Meyer:
Here was a letter from Pollsmoor Maximum prison and it was signed in hand of Mr Mandela…

Liewe Adele
My kennis van Afrikaans is baie swak en my woerdeskap laat veel ….aan te leer… dit sal seker onspoedig wees as ek verstaan as ek nou in Engels oorslaan.
Zindzi has told me several times of the interest you and Piet have shown in her problems over the past 6 years…..

V/O 6 sec
For Meyer, Winnie’s integration into their family opened a whole new world.

Meyer: She was very charming and she became a house friend this was the first to meet a black person coming to our house that was educated well informed and we started learning the outside world actually though Winnies eyes as well, she said to my parents that the longer that Nelson is staying in jail the bigger martyr he will become. Every every there was another Free Mandela campaign.

UP SOUND Tutu: “ Campaign with us for the Release of Nelson Mandela and all our political prisoners now?

V/O 7 sec
Piet and Adele’s good neighbourliness to Winnie and her children put them under the security police spotlight.

Meyer
The harassment by the police was a big thing they had a Sgt Prinsloo and he had a it of a cowboy and crooks concept he would change in to different clothes and cars, diff times of the day he even started following my mother into the grocery store and one day he crouching behind some apple boxes and the stuff fell over and he sat there sorry looking at my mother and my mother said I knew that you were following me you can get out behind the boxes now.

Meyer; You and Piet have contributed significantly to her relative safety and happiness Sincerely ….. as we get along,

V/O 8 sec
Adele and Piet didn’t speak about the letter Mandela wrote to them. Their children found it on their death.

Meyer
Up to day for me this is a really a precious part of family history.


PART 4 The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela

V/O 25 sec
Mandela never gave up trying to contact his comrades and political activists from prison. The letters he wrote to Adelaide Tambo, wife of O.R Tambo, used various nicknames and it’s not known which she received or didn’t. He must have realised his many letters to the then Bishop of Johannesburg Desmond Tutu and his wife Leah never went past the censors. In desperation, he wrote to Trevor, their son.

Title To Trevor Tutu, son of Desmond and Leah Tutu 84.08.06
…… there is virtually nothing I have not tried to contact your father but all my efforts were in vein, if this brief note reaches him he must know this is the nearest I can come to him…..

V/O
And this letter was stopped with these words from Prison Security:
“The prisoner is still trying to make contact with Bishop Desmond Tutu. He is now writing to the Bishop’s son Trevor Tutu….. This letter must not be released”.

V/O 4 and a half sec
Trevor only found about this letter a few years ago.

Trevor
It’s strange its this voice from the past this voice you admire hugely…almost like listening to Coltrane playing a haunting melody it it causes a sort of disturbance.

V/O 16 and a half sec
In August 1988 Mandela was moved from Tygerberg Hospital to Constaniaberg MediClinic.... to recuperate from tuberculosis… initially no one bar family knew…… but there was one nurse whose curiosity got the better of her.

Candie
It was a very long corridor and they closed off the fire escapes at one end and I was very curious to know what was going on, it was all hush hush, and a couple of days went by and the y put pot plants out and there was a guard and I was thinking who was in there and then the bell rang

V/O 4 sec

Unique Selling Point: For 27 years of Mandela’s life in prison his sole source of comfort, his only contact with his family and friends was the occasional visit and letters…letters he received and letters he wrote. From the very beginning Mandela was a prolific letter writer with both personal and official letters. Every letter was copied into an A4 hard covered notebook. These have been stored in boxes locked away in the State Archives. In celebration of Mandela’s 100th Birthday they are finally seeing the light of day. Summary: On July 18th, Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela would have turned 100 years. This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon. For the best part of 10 years the Nelson Mandela Foundation and South African National Archives have been collecting and assembling letters written by Nelson Mandela during his 27 years incarceration. Poignant, impassioned, gripping and always inspirational the letters – many of them never seen before by the public - provide new insight into how Mandela maintained his inner spirits while living in almost complete isolation and how he engaged with the outside world that became increasingly outraged by his plight as his imprisonment dragged into its fourth decade. A landmark book, *“The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” - the first and only authorised and authenticated collection of correspondence spanning the 27 years Mandela was held as a political prisoner - will be released a week before Mandela’s Birthday. In perfect synchronicity our documentary Mandela 100 will reveal some of the most poignant, the most witty, the most dramatic of his letters. Further information: The documentary will follow three main threads throughout its 48 minutes. Interviews with some of the younger members of the Mandela family and other individuals who featured in his life will be seamlessly weaved together to a new reveal of Nelson Mandela, the man and the life he lived. Firstly, we will trace Mandela’s life through the bigger landscape of world events, telescoping in to events where they might have influenced Mandela or the political stage he played on …for example the lead up to and the release of Mandela came at a time of extreme global change, most notably Gorbachev was dismantling the Soviet Union; in 1989 the Berlin wall fell…..Destruction of the old, heralded new beginnings. Secondly we will trace Mandela through the different stages of his life. ‘Mandela 100’ will showcase the seven stages of Nelson Mandela 1 Rolihlahla – or Trouble maker as it means: Portraying his earliest and most deeply rooted influences. The imprint of language, place and culture lie in his traditional upbringing in rural Transkei. 2 Nelson: His early years as a schoolboy and the ‘colonial’ name he was given. Embracing a colonial education, Nelson Mandela’s enduring respect for Anglo-Saxon culture is rooted in his early encounters with mission schooling, the British notions of ‘fair play’ and doing things ‘properly’ remain with him throughout his life. 3 Mr Mandela: Mandela makes his way to Johannesburg where he initially feels very much an outsider but he will soon become a charming ‘man about town’, a confident legal professional and a committed political activist. 4: Comrade, Military Commander, Fugitive: Mandela becomes a firebrand ANC leader and military commander. He goes underground, is arrested and becomes accused No 1 in the Rivonia Trial. His political activism comes at a huge personal cost. 5 Prisoner 46664: Prison shapes Mandela, inside and out. Given the harshness of prison life and the length of his incarceration, it is intriguing that he later looks back on his years in prison with some nostalgia. In a sense he remains a prisoner throughout his life, a prisoner of fame and towards the end of his life a prisoner of infirmity. 6 Mr President: With Chris Hani’s murder in April 1993 and South Africa teetering on the brink of chaos, Mandela effectively steps in to lead the country. After the first democratic elections his time as leader sparks a renewal in South Africa with the rainbow nation celebrated with optimism both locally and abroad. 7 Madiba: Post 1999, the Madiba legacy, the good, the bad and the ugly. We explore the enduring legacy of Madiba but also bring new questions to the fore as a new generation is not so enamoured with the Madiba legacy, branding him a sellout. Thirdly – the new reveal of the multitude of letters he would pen to loved ones, compatriots, prison authorities and government officials. At first he was only allowed to write and receive one letter of 500 words every six months. Even when restrictions were finally loosened regarding the length and regularity of his correspondence, his jailors continued censoring his letter for political overtones – even innocuous references. The letters will provide an intimate portrait of a political activist who was at once a devoted husband, adoring father, dedicated student (studying for a law degree behind bars) and abiding friend. A father of five when he was sentenced to life imprisonment, his letters became a critical means of parenting in absentia – particularly as he was denied visiting rights until his children reached the age of 16. Letters to comrades and old acquaintances are infused with optimism and warmth, as well as a steely resolve to stay the course. Mandela reminisces and often frets over the future yet never loses hope. ‘Mandela 100’ the documentary will get the back story of some of the most intimate, most revealing, most dramatic of these letters. Co- Author, Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela, Madiba’s granddaughter will be one of the interviews to navigate us through the letters. Some of the other interviews we aim to get from recipients of his letters or their family as the case may be…Ndaba Mandela, grandson of Mandela; the nurse who took care of Madiba in hospital; Nqaba Ngoyi ( great grandson of the late Lilian Ngoyi who he wrote to.); Tim Wilson, son-in law of the late Bram Fischer; Zwai Kente, Mandela’s nephew and son of the renowned playwright Gibson; fellow prisoner, Mac Maharaj (Mandela wrote to his wife, Tim Maharaj) the De Waals, friends of Winnie Mandela from her Brandfort days; the Tambo family (Adelaide Tambo was a recipient of letters; Tony Eprile ( son of Cecile Eprile, Golden Post editor); Andile Xaba ( son of the late Nike, Winnies sister and Marshall Xaba. Mandela in his letters is witty, clever (often cloaking references to banned colleagues through nicknames) and empathetic with others despite his own tribulations and tragedies, like the death of his mother and son, over which he anguished. And a new portrait emerges of his close relationship with Winnie Madikizela-Mandela whose own battle with the apartheid system during the same period is documented dramatically through their letters. V/O 18 sec Advocate Duma Nokwe was elected Secretary General of the ANC in 1958. In 1963 he went into exile in Zambia. Nosizwe Macamo is the youngest of his children. She was only 3 years old when she and her sisters joined their parents in exile. Nosizwe We had to be taken out of SA by people we didn’t know, so we were passed from one comrade to the next comrade to the next in the bush on foot on bicycles through Botswana where we eventually met my mother in who had left prior to our leaving us because the situation was so dire so that was how we left SA so nobody sort of left on a jet plane. V/O 9 and a half sec Duma Nokwe died in 1978. He never received any letters Mandela wrote. His family only found out about this letter just over a year ago. Sahm They were so happy that Madiba had written to him and one of the questions was so here is this freedom fighter writing to another freedom fighter both of them lawyers and he’s writing about singing and dancing. Title: To Duma Nokwe ( Gcwanini Miya) 1.1..77 Full Quality ??? Our Dear Gcwanini Now its even more difficult to follow cultural events on the mainland and even cautious comment would literally be to rush in where angels fear to tread….. Any way three musicals seem to have attracted a lot of attention recently namely. Umababatha Ipi Tombi & Meropa all of them seem tremendous in print. Nosizwe You thinking here is this man sitting in jail and he is writing about theatre and this and that ……. We came to the conclusion then this was a code but try as we might we couldn’t decipher anything… Nosizwe reads its said to have broken all records in Johannesburg when it ran for 122 weeks… and was seen by 500 thousand people I also understand in London it had similar success and three companies are presently performing in several continents. Nosizwe: Such detail and some of the words you think what was that. PART 3 The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela V/O 20 sec In the late 60’s conditions began to improve, after a visit from Opposition Member of Parliament Helen Suzman. Prisoners were now allowed to receive and write one letter, and receive visitors, every three months. Amina Cachalia’s son Ghaleb was a young boy when Mandela was sent to Robben Island. Ghaleb I am sitting here scores of letters written in Nelson’s tiny print and he say’s You say you and Yusuf are lonely people without the kids since when K was 5 was m was 4 when I last saw you but the baby you nursed on your lap was neither K or the sister but my friend Yusuf the giant. It’s never wise for those who are inside to fight against those who are free V/O 5 sec Yusuf and Amina Cachalia were friends and comrades with Mandela in the struggle. Ghaleb There was always political talk in the dining room the kitchen and Mandela’s name always was present I was 4/5 year’s old that’s when I began to remember things, and I can recall the excitement in the 70’s when a letter would arrive and my parents would read it and scour it for hidden meaning and the like. Ghaleb I also think that there were probably political reasons for that the letters went to my mum and not my dad because my dad was clearly house arrested during that period and I suppose he wanted the letters to come across as a family friendly letter but as always hidden messages put into the letters. To Joyce Sikhhakane : comrade of Winnie Mandela. January 1 1971 My dear Nomvula For you and John is it true can you two really do this to me without so much as giving me a hint a hint missed heaps of meat and pudding at the engagement party V/O 15 sec Mandela’s letter to struggle activist and journalist Joyce Sikhakane-Rankin, whom he calls Nomvula, is infectious in its sense of joy and celebration. Joyce was marrying John Faduna, a relative of his. … To you wedding I would have been accepted just as I am, without having to sport a frock coat, starched shirt & top hat. What is even more important to me, your wedding is one occasion where I could have shined at last. I rehearse daily on a penny whistle with more practice I could have tried Handels Messiah on it on the great day. V/ O 12 and a half sec Change graphic people to black check people visuals But Mandela’s congratulations were premature. He was only to know later that the Special Branch called her out for breaking her banning order; they said the marriage was invalid. Joyce They said they were going to charge me…So the marriage was invalid…because I had broken the banning orders that’s the way they interpreted it. You feel dammed what ever they say you are dammed, I just continued with my life, V/O 12 sec In his letters to prison authorities Mandela insisted prisoners’ rights were upheld …and the degradation of black prisoners was a cause he fiercely pursued. The Commissioner of Prisons 12th July 1976 Pretoria In this country only white prisoners have the right to sleep in pyjamas…Black prisoners here sleep naked with only blankets as a cover…For thirteen years I have slept naked on a cement floor that becomes damp and cold during the rainy season. Andile It was just a system that de humanising him and he refused he said I want pyjamas I want long trousers. V/O 7 and a half sec It was in their deliberate isolation of the political prisoners, that the South African apartheid regime made a crucial mistake. Mac Instead of dispersing us throughout the prison system it put us together and it had common law prisoners there to do cooking of food and all that when it found we were communicating with them and finding sympathy with them, it removed them too. when they removed them what else was left except to study intensely what was happening both to equip yourselves so that when you got released you went into battle and those who left behind to continue teaching the others and share the knowledge. V/O 11 sec On May the 16th 1977, Winnie Mandela was banished to the dusty town of Brandfort in the Orange Free State. She was there for 8 years. Sahm: This book for me is full of all sorts of serendipities links and when Winnie Mandela was banished to Brandfort, Piet De Waal was the town lawyer and his wife `Adele befriended Winnie and was incredibly helpful to her in this horrible hostile situation. Meyer: My mother invited her to the house and Winnie came to the house and my mother came to the door and said this is my house please come and make use of the music and books and make yourself comfortable. V/O 14 and a half sec It’s easy to forget the laws that kept South Africans living apart, like the curfew. In Brandfort a siren went off just before 9pm …and every black person that didn’t live in the backyard of a white house, had to be out of town. Meyer If you think back maybe you can say it was brave but I think they were just oblivious of black and white for them it was a person who came from a different environment …I don’t think she had running water, it was like dumping her into a terrible space and my mother realised that here is a person in need … To Adele de Waal, a friend of his wife Winnie Mandela 29.8.83 Meyer: Here was a letter from Pollsmoor Maximum prison and it was signed in hand of Mr Mandela… Liewe Adele My kennis van Afrikaans is baie swak en my woerdeskap laat veel ….aan te leer… dit sal seker onspoedig wees as ek verstaan as ek nou in Engels oorslaan. Zindzi has told me several times of the interest you and Piet have shown in her problems over the past 6 years….. V/O 6 sec For Meyer, Winnie’s integration into their family opened a whole new world. Meyer: She was very charming and she became a house friend this was the first to meet a black person coming to our house that was educated well informed and we started learning the outside world actually though Winnies eyes as well, she said to my parents that the longer that Nelson is staying in jail the bigger martyr he will become. Every every there was another Free Mandela campaign. UP SOUND Tutu: “ Campaign with us for the Release of Nelson Mandela and all our political prisoners now? V/O 7 sec Piet and Adele’s good neighbourliness to Winnie and her children put them under the security police spotlight. Meyer The harassment by the police was a big thing they had a Sgt Prinsloo and he had a it of a cowboy and crooks concept he would change in to different clothes and cars, diff times of the day he even started following my mother into the grocery store and one day he crouching behind some apple boxes and the stuff fell over and he sat there sorry looking at my mother and my mother said I knew that you were following me you can get out behind the boxes now. Meyer; You and Piet have contributed significantly to her relative safety and happiness Sincerely ….. as we get along, V/O 8 sec Adele and Piet didn’t speak about the letter Mandela wrote to them. Their children found it on their death. Meyer Up to day for me this is a really a precious part of family history. PART 4 The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela V/O 25 sec Mandela never gave up trying to contact his comrades and political activists from prison. The letters he wrote to Adelaide Tambo, wife of O.R Tambo, used various nicknames and it’s not known which she received or didn’t. He must have realised his many letters to the then Bishop of Johannesburg Desmond Tutu and his wife Leah never went past the censors. In desperation, he wrote to Trevor, their son. Title To Trevor Tutu, son of Desmond and Leah Tutu 84.08.06 …… there is virtually nothing I have not tried to contact your father but all my efforts were in vein, if this brief note reaches him he must know this is the nearest I can come to him….. V/O And this letter was stopped with these words from Prison Security: “The prisoner is still trying to make contact with Bishop Desmond Tutu. He is now writing to the Bishop’s son Trevor Tutu….. This letter must not be released”. V/O 4 and a half sec Trevor only found about this letter a few years ago. Trevor It’s strange its this voice from the past this voice you admire hugely…almost like listening to Coltrane playing a haunting melody it it causes a sort of disturbance. V/O 16 and a half sec In August 1988 Mandela was moved from Tygerberg Hospital to Constaniaberg MediClinic.... to recuperate from tuberculosis… initially no one bar family knew…… but there was one nurse whose curiosity got the better of her. Candie It was a very long corridor and they closed off the fire escapes at one end and I was very curious to know what was going on, it was all hush hush, and a couple of days went by and the y put pot plants out and there was a guard and I was thinking who was in there and then the bell rang V/O 4 sec And this was Candie’s moment to meet the mystery patient. Candie I didn’t recognise him immediately I walked in and said Hello I am Sister Lawless and can I help you and he said hello I am Nelson Mandela in that voice that he’s got he has got that distinct voice. Pam C was our sister in charge at the time and she knew I was a bit of a wild card and I remember rolling my eyes and she was well know that you have met the patient you may continue looking after him as well. V/O 10 sec The apartheid government banned photographs of Nelson Mandela …but Candie’s fiancée, Trevor got one of his first waves. Candie: Trevor was can he wave to me and I said No he can’t he’s not allowed to be seen outside the hospital. He said come on ask him so I went up and said Mr Mandela, I have a favour to ask you, would you be prepared to wave out the window and he said yes he would I told Trevor we were like what if he’s caught what if there are reporters around, they are going to get a picture and he’s going to get in trouble so we go downstairs and I said look up there that’s the window and then the next thing out came this brown hand just waving it was so funny…laughing I said that’s him that’s him…Laughs V/O 8 sec Nelson Mandela was now 70 years old, he had been in prison for 26 years, he had twelve grandchildren. Candie: We spoke about his family, we spoke about Winnie his children and how sad he was that he had never held them for so long he missed children he missed their laughter. V/O 8 sec Months later Candie received a card from Nelson Mandela, she wrote back and he replied with a letter. To: Candie Lawless, a nurse who took care of him at Constatiaberg MediClinic 4.4.89 Dear Candie ……..I am even more pleased to hear that you and Trevor are engaged…if he had not proposed by now I would have urged you to seize the bull by the horn and propose to him after all – I love this sentence- the acceptance of the principal of the equality of the sexes gives you that right when a young man drags his feet…. V/O 13 sec 1989 and President P.W Botha was talking about the release of Nelson Mandela. A secret meeting between Mandela and The Groot Krokodil took place on July the fifth that same year. A photograph was taken…. To the commissioner of prisons 17 July 1989 PERSONAL AND CONFIDENTIAL pg 535 I trust that the photographs taken on July 5th 1989 will not be published or distributed without consulting the parties involved. I hope to have a further discussion with you on this matter in due course. V/O 8 and a half sec The letter Tim Wilson, Director of the Alex Health Clinic received from Mandela in 1989 could not have come at a better time. Sound Up V/O 11 sec Mandela was now in Victor Verster Prison, the country was in a State of Emergency and Alexandra township was a hot bed of violence and state sponsored terror. Tim I wrote to him in 89 we were about to celebrate our 60th anniversary as a clinic and it was a tough time. When the police in 86 demanded patient records we refused so we continued with that attitude we stand with the people of Alex and we are not a government service V/O 11 sec Mandela’s reply came 4 days after the clinic was petrol bombed and lives were lost. The attack was by the police - it came out later at the TRC hearings. To Tim Wilson Director: Alexandra Health Centre and University Clinic (known mostly as Alex Health Centre) 23.7.89 Dear Tim The Alexandra Health Centre is a unique project in more senses than one for one thing it brings hope where there was despair and even life where death would have triumphed Tim It was extraordinary and it really was at the time I wondered myself if I had been pushing people too hard If I had put people at risk and here this letter of support in support of the clinic but also on support of me. And I think it helped all of us to keep going Part 5 The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela V/O 23 sec The first offer to release Mandela came in 1974. The condition? - he live in the Transkei! His rejection was the first of many. In the 80’s, in discussions, negotiations and letters to government, Mandela successfully pressed for the release of his comrades first. Denis Goldberg was released in 1985. Denis My wife was allowed 2 visits to me one after about 4 years and one after 7 years and then for 14 years I didn’t see her and when I came out of prison she said is this what I waited for this old man with no hair, gold rimmed glasses, looks like his father three weeks later she said shall we try to live together but she said there are conditions. I would have said yes to anything at that point because I came off the plane and she smiled at me and that was enough. Well our children and our wives paid the price I have to say and our movement doesn’t like to acknowledge it enough. V/O 7 and a half sec 7 sec On February the second, 1990 F. W. de Klerk played his trump card, the release of Nelson Mandela. Up Sound V/O 11 sec And seven days later, Nelson Mandela emerged from Victor Verster Prison arm in arm with Winnie…Free at last. Swati I think sometimes people forget that my grandparents were married and he loved her and she loved him and they had this incredible bond, they were more drawn together when she was in solitary confinement and he was on Robben Island then when they were actually physically together that says a lot of people bring bonded by something like that. Ghaleb The worlds press descended on SA and some Indian media people they asked me to show them around and my mother was waiting at Tutu’s house so I drove to the house with these media people and we met Nelson after all this time and sitting and talking to him in the flesh was amazing and then my mother and I said to him that the worlds press was there with all these great anchor men and it was a big tussle to who was going to get the first interview so we said to him the government of India has always stood by you and the ANC throughout the years we think you should give the first interview to them. He said Of Course Of course …they were bowled over, and Ted Koppel and all these people were aghast that these lowly Indians media people in their minds scored the first interview. V/O 14 sec Nosizwe and her mother returned to South Africa, they had permission to bury her late cousin’s body in Cape Town. Their meeting with Mandela was serendipitous. Nosizwe And as we get to Johannesburg we were advised that this was the end of the journey for your coffin we said No No the tickets and everything we are taking the body to Cape Town the authorities said No No the body stops here Can you imagine my mother hasn’t been back since we left in 1964 this is the first time in 1991 we are at a loss what should we do and you will not believe it and as we are standing there at the airport and we see some commotion happening and when I look I’m like NO mum look tall figure that’s Uncle Nel and Mummy says no it cant be where and she looks and says My goodness its him we are standing there totally transfixed and there are a lot of people around him and it just so happens that they cross our path and then he stops he looks at my mother and goes TINI and she goes Oh Boetie and there’s hugging and he says you’re looking marvellous what is going on and she explains to him the issue and he says that’s not acceptable CAN YOU MAKE SURE MRS NOKWE GETS TO CT WITH THE PRECIOUS CARGO SHE”S CARRYING and that was that….. V/O 11 sec Mayer’s parents Piet and Adele never got to meet Mandela, they had already passed away. Adele died on the day Mandela walked free. Meyer: What I do understand from the letter he took sincere appreciation in that he listened Winnie must have told him what my parents are about and he took interests in what they did. I am pretty sure if they were still alive he would have wanted to come and meet them in Brandfort because that’s the type of person he was. V/O 5 and a half sec Mandela did reach out to Meyer and his family and invited them to tea. Meyer We walked out there felt 2 months afterwards on a clouds and UI felt like the most amazing person. V/O 11 sec Nelson and Amina shared a common history in the struggle but despite public speculation of a closer relationship, they remained friends – even after her husband Yusuf died. Gahleb My mother called my sister and I and she wanted to talk to us because she said Nelson had asked her to marry him and she said she thought about it and she told him that she didn’t want to get married firstly because she had just lost my father recently and secondly she said she wanted to live a life outside the limelight and then she said who wants another old man in your life. V/O 9 sec For Mac, Mandela’s greatest moment came after his son Makgatho died of AIDS-related complications in 2005. Mac I remember the day of his death I had visited the hospital visited Makgatho but the day he died he still had this capacity to hold back his grief but if you look at that clip you will see grief written all over his face. UP SOUND That meeting people who were saying don’ts say he was saying we have to say to the public he died of Aids and that’s why his knowledge of AIDs show she turned it around and that’s why when he retired the one thing he has said he acknowledging inadequate attention he gave to the of AIDS. V/O 15 and a half sec But in the post Mandela era, political freedom has not led to economic freedom for the majority. Poverty has in fact increased and a new generation of marginalised youth are calling Mandela a sell out. Ghaleb To call people like NM a sellout would be akin to calling people like Ghandi a sell out, would be akin to calling people like Martin Luther King a sell out these people were not sell outs they were men and women of their times they stood their ground and tried to put forward a future for all not a future for some. Swati If drive through Diepsloot, when I drive through Soweto, the poorest parts in this country I understand how people feel that way, .so what freedom what are you talking about like where is it I don’t see it I don’t feel it. A very few people have enjoyed it but the masses in this country have not so I don’t think its anything to do with him being a sell out rather that how was our freedom and peace negotiated. Ghaleb If Mandela was alive now he would look back and say we failed. Up SOUND Mandela: Now one of the temptations of a leader who has been elected unopposed is that he may use that powerful position to settle scores with those of his detractors….and surround himself with yes men and women…. V/O Perhaps now more than ever is the time to relook at Mandela’s values. Values reflected in his letters - tolerance, justice, caring and forgiveness. Title: To Joy Motsieloa, his friend 17.02.86 Pollsmoor Prison Up Sound: When a man commits himself to the type of life he has lived for 45 years. V/O 9 sec Four years before Mandela was released, he wrote to a friend expressing his absolute faith in his chosen path. If I had been able to forsee all that has since happened, I would have certainly made the same decision, so I believe at least. But that decision would have certainly been far more daunting Sahm It was a very powerful letter, in 1986 in a state of emergency the country was quiet literally in flames I can’t help but picture him as a much older man writing to his friend if I had the chance to do the same thing I would even though knowing what I know now and I think that describes exactly who he really was and why he was such a powerful person. V/O 7 sec Mandela’s last free words before his long incarceration was his moment of truth. Up SOUND V/O 6 sec And these were the same ideals he expressed towards the end of his life. …where all South Africans are equal

metadata.Unique Selling Point: For 27 years of Mandela’s life in prison his sole source of comfort, his only contact with his family and friends was the occasional visit and letters…letters he received and letters he wrote. From the very beginning Mandela was a prolific letter writer with both personal and official letters. Every letter was copied into an A4 hard covered notebook. These have been stored in boxes locked away in the State Archives. In celebration of Mandela’s 100th Birthday they are finally seeing the light of day.
metadata.Summary: On July 18th, Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela would have turned 100 years. This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon. For the best part of 10 years the Nelson Mandela Foundation and South African National Archives have been collecting and assembling letters written by Nelson Mandela during his 27 years incarceration. Poignant, impassioned, gripping and always inspirational the letters – many of them never seen before by the public - provide new insight into how Mandela maintained his inner spirits while living in almost complete isolation and how he engaged with the outside world that became increasingly outraged by his plight as his imprisonment dragged into its fourth decade. A landmark book, *“The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” - the first and only authorised and authenticated collection of correspondence spanning the 27 years Mandela was held as a political prisoner - will be released a week before Mandela’s Birthday. In perfect synchronicity our documentary Mandela 100 will reveal some of the most poignant, the most witty, the most dramatic of his letters.
metadata.Further information: The documentary will follow three main threads throughout its 48 minutes. Interviews with some of the younger members of the Mandela family and other individuals who featured in his life will be seamlessly weaved together to a new reveal of Nelson Mandela, the man and the life he lived. Firstly, we will trace Mandela’s life through the bigger landscape of world events, telescoping in to events where they might have influenced Mandela or the political stage he played on …for example the lead up to and the release of Mandela came at a time of extreme global change, most notably Gorbachev was dismantling the Soviet Union; in 1989 the Berlin wall fell…..Destruction of the old, heralded new beginnings. Secondly we will trace Mandela through the different stages of his life. ‘Mandela 100’ will showcase the seven stages of Nelson Mandela 1 Rolihlahla – or Trouble maker as it means: Portraying his earliest and most deeply rooted influences. The imprint of language, place and culture lie in his traditional upbringing in rural Transkei. 2 Nelson: His early years as a schoolboy and the ‘colonial’ name he was given. Embracing a colonial education, Nelson Mandela’s enduring respect for Anglo-Saxon culture is rooted in his early encounters with mission schooling, the British notions of ‘fair play’ and doing things ‘properly’ remain with him throughout his life. 3 Mr Mandela: Mandela makes his way to Johannesburg where he initially feels very much an outsider but he will soon become a charming ‘man about town’, a confident legal professional and a committed political activist. 4: Comrade, Military Commander, Fugitive: Mandela becomes a firebrand ANC leader and military commander. He goes underground, is arrested and becomes accused No 1 in the Rivonia Trial. His political activism comes at a huge personal cost. 5 Prisoner 46664: Prison shapes Mandela, inside and out. Given the harshness of prison life and the length of his incarceration, it is intriguing that he later looks back on his years in prison with some nostalgia. In a sense he remains a prisoner throughout his life, a prisoner of fame and towards the end of his life a prisoner of infirmity. 6 Mr President: With Chris Hani’s murder in April 1993 and South Africa teetering on the brink of chaos, Mandela effectively steps in to lead the country. After the first democratic elections his time as leader sparks a renewal in South Africa with the rainbow nation celebrated with optimism both locally and abroad. 7 Madiba: Post 1999, the Madiba legacy, the good, the bad and the ugly. We explore the enduring legacy of Madiba but also bring new questions to the fore as a new generation is not so enamoured with the Madiba legacy, branding him a sellout. Thirdly – the new reveal of the multitude of letters he would pen to loved ones, compatriots, prison authorities and government officials. At first he was only allowed to write and receive one letter of 500 words every six months. Even when restrictions were finally loosened regarding the length and regularity of his correspondence, his jailors continued censoring his letter for political overtones – even innocuous references. The letters will provide an intimate portrait of a political activist who was at once a devoted husband, adoring father, dedicated student (studying for a law degree behind bars) and abiding friend. A father of five when he was sentenced to life imprisonment, his letters became a critical means of parenting in absentia – particularly as he was denied visiting rights until his children reached the age of 16. Letters to comrades and old acquaintances are infused with optimism and warmth, as well as a steely resolve to stay the course. Mandela reminisces and often frets over the future yet never loses hope. ‘Mandela 100’ the documentary will get the back story of some of the most intimate, most revealing, most dramatic of these letters. Co- Author, Zamaswazi Dlamini- Mandela, Madiba’s granddaughter will be one of the interviews to navigate us through the letters. Some of the other interviews we aim to get from recipients of his letters or their family as the case may be…Ndaba Mandela, grandson of Mandela; the nurse who took care of Madiba in hospital; Nqaba Ngoyi ( great grandson of the late Lilian Ngoyi who he wrote to.); Tim Wilson, son-in law of the late Bram Fischer; Zwai Kente, Mandela’s nephew and son of the renowned playwright Gibson; fellow prisoner, Mac Maharaj (Mandela wrote to his wife, Tim Maharaj) the De Waals, friends of Winnie Mandela from her Brandfort days; the Tambo family (Adelaide Tambo was a recipient of letters; Tony Eprile ( son of Cecile Eprile, Golden Post editor); Andile Xaba ( son of the late Nike, Winnies sister and Marshall Xaba. Mandela in his letters is witty, clever (often cloaking references to banned colleagues through nicknames) and empathetic with others despite his own tribulations and tragedies, like the death of his mother and son, over which he anguished. And a new portrait emerges of his close relationship with Winnie Madikizela-Mandela whose own battle with the apartheid system during the same period is documented dramatically through their letters.
